Multifamily Google Ads: When Paid Search Earns Its Budget

Nov 2, 2026Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM

Multifamily Google Ads earn their budget when you have homes to lease now and not enough organic visibility to reach renters who do not yet know your name. That is nearly always true in a lease up and only sometimes true at a stabilized community, so the two should never run the same plan.

Many accounts I see are not built around that difference. They run the same structure and the same monthly number all year, and the report goes out looking healthy either way.

Why does a lease up need paid search?

A new community starts with very little for Google to weigh. Google names relevance, distance and prominence as the local ranking inputs, and says more reviews and positive ratings can help. A building that opened last month has few reviews and no history, and there is no way to pay for a better local ranking. Ads are the one surface where you can appear for "two bedroom apartments" in your city on day one.

The market raises the stakes. Apartment List put the national concession rate, the share of properties advertising a concession worth at least a month of rent, at 31.3% in September 2026. Your renter is comparing you with other new buildings holding offers of their own, which we wrote about in why concessions are a signal.

Three things should be true before a lease up spends a dollar. The landing page must state the current offer and real floor plans. The phone must have a plan for tour hours. And someone must be watching what rivals change each week, because a message that worked in March may be stale by May.

Paid search should also have an exit plan. As LocalLift work and reviews build organic and Maps presence, the ad budget can shift from "be seen at all" toward the specific homes still open. A lease up that ends as dependent on ads as it began has missed part of the point.

When does paid search earn its budget at a stabilized community?

A stabilized community should already be visible for many searches. Paid search then becomes a targeted tool, and it earns its place in specific moments:

  • One floor plan has real exposure, or a block of move outs is coming.
  • A rival nearby has opened or added an offer and is pulling tours.
  • You are losing ground in a part of your trade area that organic and Maps cannot cover soon.

It earns less when it runs at a flat level all year, with most of the money landing on your own name. Bidding on your community name when you already rank first can buy clicks you would have received anyway. There are fair reasons to do some of it, such as a rival bidding on your name, so test it instead of assuming. At a small budget, though, ask how much is left to reach a renter who has never heard of you.

What does a lead actually cost?

LocaliQ's 2026 benchmarks for real estate search ads, from nearly 900 campaigns running April 2025 through March 2026, show a typical cost per click of $3.22, a conversion rate of 3.70% and a cost per lead of $102.51. That category is broader than apartments, so treat it as a rough yardstick. At that rate, $1,500 of real media buys about 15 leads.

Now look at what that hides. Here is one community report we reviewed this year:

  • The monthly budget was about $2,690, and roughly $1,550 of it reached Google. So about 42% of that figure never bought an ad.
  • The month showed 14 acquisitions, every one a phone call, since a call counted whether or not anyone answered.
  • Property wide, the call log showed 29 calls, 21 missed and 4 recorded as lead calls.
  • The clicks themselves were healthy, and website form fills were zero.

Bids were the wrong place to look in that account. Traffic was arriving, the page was not converting it, and most calls were not reaching anyone. Check traffic against conversion before anyone touches bids, and share a missed call pattern with the onsite team as a joint problem, early and in writing. Otherwise an agency can double the calls and still get blamed when leases hold flat.

Who controls what your ad says?

Google's automation is getting broader. Its help page on text customization, part of AI Max, describes a feature that writes headlines and descriptions from your landing page, existing ads and keywords. That can help some advertisers. For an apartment community with changing specials, it raises a fair question about what gets shown and who approved it. We have seen an ad serve a photo of a different community, which is a rough thing to explain to an owner.

Housing also has its own rules. Google's policy blocks targeting housing ads by age, gender, parental status, marital status or ZIP code in the US, so check that any plan you are shown respects them.

Our approach is called Verified Reach. Every ad is approved by the client before it serves, and the media budget stays visible as its own line. Renter Signal, our call intelligence, then tells you what people ask once they phone. You should expect a plain view of what your ad says and what it cost, from any partner.

Which numbers should you ignore?

Google describes Quality Score as a diagnostic tool and says it "isn't an input in the ad auction." I hold the full set of Google marketing certifications, and I still would not let a score like that lead a monthly report. Click through rate and clicks can also look fine while nothing happens downstream.

The useful line is cost per qualified call or tour, by community, over a long enough stretch. We read an account at 30 days and judge it at 90. A click this week is rarely a lease this month, so be cautious of anyone promising leases in the first few weeks.

What should you ask about your own account?

Start with what Google says you have a right to know: clicks, impressions and total cost. Then ask how much of the budget was media and how much was fee, whose card is on the account, and who keeps it if you part ways. A fee set as a percentage of spend pays more each time the budget goes up, so note who is recommending the raise. Questions we hear

How much should an apartment community spend on Google Ads?

There is no honest universal figure. Tie it to how many homes need leasing, how competitive the market is and how visible you already are. A lease up generally justifies more than a stabilized community in the same market.

Should we bid on our own community name?

Test it. If you already rank first and no rival is bidding on your name, those clicks may have reached you anyway. At small budgets, that money may do more on searches from renters who do not know you.

Can we target by ZIP code or age?

Not for US housing ads. Google's policy blocks targeting by age, gender, parental status, marital status and ZIP code.

How long before we can judge Google Ads?

We take a first real read at 30 days and a verdict at 90. Calls and cost per call show up well before leases do.

Can paid search replace SEO for a stabilized property?

It can cover a gap, and it stops the day the budget stops. Organic and Maps presence keep working when the budget pauses, which is why we treat ads as a tool within a wider plan.
